title: The services page a community sports club actually needs
metaTitle: The sessions page a sports club needs
excerpt: List the sessions a person can join, in words they already use. Each one needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step to membership or the schedule.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. A clear menu of distinct things, which is what a sessions page should be.
caption: Folded shirts, hanging jackets, and shelves in a clothing shop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a session block contain?
faqs.answer: Name the session in the member's words, say what the hour is for, say what it will not do, and link to membership or the schedule. A parent should be able to match a child to a block from the ages, the night, and the price shape. Vague capability cards do not survive that test.

faqs.question: How many ways to take part belong on one page?
faqs.answer: A handful of real sessions can share one menu. Give a session its own page when it has its own timetable, fee, and rules, such as a junior section. The index still has to stand alone, so the right door is obvious before the click.

faqs.question: What headings fail a new member?
faqs.answer: Headings fail when you can swap the sentences between social and squad and nothing breaks. They also fail when they use internal program names nobody says at the desk. Read the headings aloud. A new member should be able to point at one.

sources.title: Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
A community sports club services page should list what a member can actually join, in the words they already use. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step: see membership or the schedule. A grid of vague capabilities leaves them guessing which box is for them.

The page is a menu of ways to take part. Social, coached, junior, competitive, or a course with a start date. If a line on the menu could describe any club in the country, it is not yet an offer.

## Write the menu in the member's words

People do not arrive looking for "athlete development pathways" or "community engagement streams." They arrive looking for a Tuesday hit, a junior session, a course for beginners, or a squad that plays in the league. Use those words as the titles of the sections. The club can keep its internal names in the registration system. The page should use the names a new person would say at the front desk.

Google's guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive, concise titles, and it warns against boilerplate that makes two pages impossible to tell apart. The same standard belongs on the page itself. "Seniors," "Juniors," and "Social" are distinct. "Program one," "Program two," and "Program three" are boilerplate. If every block uses the same heading style and the same empty adjective, the menu looks longer and means less.

One page can hold the whole menu when the club has a handful of ways to take part. Split into separate pages when an offer has its own timetable, its own fee shape, and its own rules, such as a junior section with safeguarding notes. The index page still has to stand alone. A person should know which door is theirs before they click.

Ballarat Box Sports, a public Hanabi project, is a community sports brand site. The relevant lesson for this page is restraint in naming. A sports brand can sound like the room it comes from. It does not need a catalogue of abstract strengths. Look at public work for tone. Do not invent claims about what that site converts.

## Outcome: what changes for the person who joins

Each offer should say what the person leaves with, or what their week contains. A beginner course ends with a person who can join a social session safely. A junior session gives a child a coached hour and a parent a clear pickup time. A senior training night is for people who already play and want sharper sessions before the weekend match.

Write that outcome in a sentence, under the name of the offer. Avoid a slogan that could sit on any of the blocks. If you can swap the sentences between "social" and "squad" and nothing breaks, both sentences are still empty.

The outcome can include level. No experience required. You should be comfortable at social pace. Selection applies. Saying the level is an outcome too: it tells the reader whether they will be out of their depth or under-used. Clubs lose beginners by sounding elite, and they lose serious players by sounding like a drop-in. The sentence prevents both losses.

A short proof helps when you have it. The coach's name and the fact they hold the relevant qualification. The league the squad plays in. The number of weeks in the course, if the course has a fixed length. These are facts the club already knows. They are more persuasive than a stock line about passion.

## Boundary: what this offer will not do

Every offer needs an edge, or it expands until it disappoints. The social session is for play, and it is the wrong place to demand tactical drills. The beginner course does not include match selection. The junior hour ends at the stated time, and it is supervised, and it is for the ages printed on the block. The squad trains for the fixture list, and paying the fee is the start of that, subject to the selection rule you already publish on the fees page.

Write the boundary as a plain limit. People trust a club that says what the hour is. They distrust a club that implies every session is all things. A boundary also protects volunteers. A coach who was booked to run a social hit should not discover three parents who expected one-to-one coaching because the website was dreamy.

If two offers overlap, say how to choose. "Start in the beginner course if you have not played. Move to social when the coach suggests it. The squad is a conversation after you have been around for a term." That is a path. A grid of six identical cards is a wall.

Equipment can be part of the boundary. Bats provided. Boats provided for the course, bring your own once you join the squad. Indoor shoes required, no outdoor soles on the hall floor. These lines save the first session from being a lecture.

## The next step is membership or the schedule

Each block ends the same way, in the same words the rest of the site uses. See membership or the schedule. The link can be specific: the Tuesday social times, the junior fees, the squad registration. The label should still be recognizable, so a person who saw the homepage button recognizes the door.

Do not end a block with "find out more" if the more is another page of adjectives. Link to the fact that completes the decision. Time. Price. How to start. If the schedule is one page with anchors, link the anchor. If registration opens on a date, the next step can be "fees open on 1 September; see the schedule meanwhile."

A parent reading on a phone in the car park should be able to match a child to a block in under a minute. That means the ages, the night, and the price shape are on the block or one tap away, in the same words the coach uses at the door. If those facts live only in a PDF named "info pack," the menu has failed the person who was ready to decide.

A single primary action per offer is enough. A second link, such as emailing a coach, can sit as a quiet line for people with a specific question. If every block offers four buttons, nobody knows the real one. The real one for a member deciding whether to join is to see membership or the schedule.

Repeat the action at the bottom of the page for the person who scrolled the whole menu and is ready. Same words. Same destination pattern.

## Cut the capability grid

Agency sites and software sites often use a grid of capabilities: strategy, community, performance, wellbeing. A club that copies that grid describes a mood. It does not describe Thursday. Replace each box with an offer a person can attend, or delete it.

Test the page by reading only the headings aloud. If a new member could point at one and say "that one," the menu works. If they would still need to ask a volunteer what the words mean, the headings are still internal.

Watch for offers that exist only because a template had six slots. An empty "corporate events" card, or a "personal training" card nobody is qualified to sell, makes the real sessions look less serious. Publish the sessions you run this season. Add a card when a new session has a coach, a time, and a fee.

Photography should agree with the menu. A junior block needs a junior session, with consent handled before the picture is used. A social block needs social play, slightly imperfect, recognizably fun. One heroic crop reused on every card tells the reader the offers are interchangeable. They came to the page to learn that the offers are distinct.

## How the page stays true after launch

The services page rots when the season changes and the cards do not. A course that ended in June should come off the menu or be marked as the next intake. A squad that folded should not keep recruiting from a forgotten URL. Assign a person, often the same person who updates the schedule, to read the menu at the start of each term.

Build it so that edit is dull. Headings, a short outcome, a short boundary, a link. On a Hanabi-built marketing site the stack is the one the studio actually ships: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, with content a small team can change. The technology matters only because the menu must be editable when the term changes. A page that needs a designer to remove a finished course will keep advertising the finished course.

Keep the tone level. The club can be warm without writing a manifesto above the menu. One sentence at the top can say who the club is for. Then the menu. People who want the origin story can have it on the about page, after they know there is a session for them.

## The page that says who stands behind the menu

A clear menu creates a new question. Who runs these sessions, and why should a stranger trust them with a child, a body, or a season fee. Answer that with people and responsibility, and skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision. That is [how a community sports club should write an about page](/blog/how-a-community-sports-club-should-write-an-about-page).

If the menu is the piece you want help shaping, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful brief is the list of sessions you really run, in the words members use.
